CausalChain: Overexpression of MALAT1 under metabolic stress -> Formation of a stable, inducible triple helix structure (enhanced by adaptor proteins) -> Conditional scaffold function for localized recruitment of glycolytic enzymes AND integration with gene regulatory signals -> Enhanced local glycolytic activity and metabolic plasticity under stress -> Synergistic contribution to tumor metabolic reprogramming -> Disruption of the triple helix via small molecules (structure-based design) -> Inhibition of enzyme recruitment and regulatory interactions -> Reversal of stress-induced metabolic adaptations -> Reduced tumor progression in metabolically demanding environments
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in response to metabolic stress, overexpressed MALAT1 folds into a stable triple helix configuration that acts as a conditional metabolic regulator by orchestrating the assembly of glycolytic enzymes through direct and adaptor-mediated interactions, and concurrently modulating gene regulatory networks. This dual functionality enables a refined spatial organization of metabolic machinery that enhances glycolytic flux and confers metabolic plasticity in cancer cells. Importantly, targeted disruption of this triple helix using structure-based small molecules—validated via CRISPR perturbation, high-resolution structural imaging, and single-cell metabolomic profiling—will specifically impair the adaptive metabolic reprogramming of tumor cells without affecting baseline cellular functions in normal tissues.
Abstract: Recent evidence suggests that long noncoding RNAs may exert multifaceted roles in cancer beyond classical gene regulation. In this study, we propose that under specific metabolic stress conditions, overexpressed MALAT1 adopts a highly stable triple helix conformation that not only facilitates localized assembly of glycolytic enzymes through specific RNA‐protein interactions (possibly mediated by adaptor proteins) but also interfaces with its well‐established gene regulatory functions. This conditional assembly enhances glycolytic flux and metabolic plasticity specifically in cancer cells, particularly under hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, or chemotherapeutic stress. By integrating CRISPR-based perturbation, high-resolution structural analyses, and single-cell metabolomics, we aim to dissect how selective disruption of the MALAT1 triple helix—via structure-based small molecule inhibitors—specifically impairs the localized enzyme recruitment and downstream metabolic adaptations. This refined model ascribes an additional, novel layer of metabolic regulation to MALAT1 in tumor progression, presenting new opportunities for targeted anticancer strategies with minimized effects on normal tissues.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that the MALAT1 triple helix conditionally regulates metabolic plasticity via enzyme assembly under stress. The refined hypothesis retains this core causal chain but expands it by (1) incorporating the role of adaptor proteins and integration with gene regulatory functions to account for broader influences on cellular metabolism, (2) specifying stress conditions such as hypoxia and chemotherapeutic challenges to clarify when this mechanism is activated, and (3) emphasizing the use of contemporary technologies (CRISPR tools, high-resolution structural analyses, and single-cell metabolomics) to validate the mechanism. These modifications enhance mechanistic detail, experimental feasibility, and practical therapeutic applicability.
